summary: Examines the problems with packet size when tunnels such as IP-in-IP are used in the middle of a network. It covers whether large packets are fragmented and reassembled, whether Path MTU Discovery is used, and how to avoid the problem operationally, and compares solutions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A tunnel is a narrow pipe, so big packages may not fit. This note looks at ways to cut them up or avoid shipping big ones.

questions: how do tunnels handle large packets
when should you use path mtu discovery in tunnels
subtitle: Solving the packet size problem when tunneling between routers

tldr.problem: When tunnels like IP-in-IP encapsulation are deployed between routers in a network, they add overhead that may exceed the path's maximum transmission unit (MTU), forcing packets to be fragmented or dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines four approaches: fragmenting and reassembling packets at tunnel endpoints, signalling sources to reduce packet size via Path MTU Discovery, ensuring the backbone network has enough MTU, or fragmenting inner packets before encapsulation.
tldr.outcome: No single solution works universally; the best approach depends on the deployment scenario, whether IPv4 or IPv6 is used, and the network's capabilities.

today: RFC 4459 is an Informational RFC published in April 2006. It remains the definitive analysis of MTU and fragmentation problems in tunneled networks. Its conclusions remain relevant: deployment choices are case-specific, and IPv4 and IPv6 require different strategies.

sections.title: Tunneling and the MTU Problem
sections.content:
Tunneling protocols such as IP-in-IP, Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP), and IPsec wrap packets inside other packets to encapsulate and forward traffic across a network. Tunnels can run between hosts, between a host and a router, or between routers.

When a tunnel encapsulates a packet, it adds header bytes to the packet. If the encapsulated packet exceeds the smallest MTU along the tunnel path, it will not fit in a single link and must either be fragmented (split into smaller pieces) or dropped. This memo focuses on router-to-router tunneling, where the problem is most difficult because the tunnel must handle traffic from many sources.
sections.eli5: Tunneling wraps a package in extra packaging. But if the total is too big for the tunnel, you have to either cut it into pieces or throw it away.

sections.title: Why This Is a Problem
sections.content:
Fragmentation and reassembly seem like an obvious solution but create serious issues: they waste bandwidth because each fragment needs its own header; they require significant processing power; and at line speeds (gigabits per second), reassembly buffers become prohibitively large.

IPv4 has an additional critical flaw: the 16-bit identification field used to reassemble fragments will wrap (reset) when reassembling many packets, causing data from different packets to be incorrectly combined. This risks data corruption.

Other naive solutions have problems too. Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) to signal sources is unreliable in IPv4 due to firewalls blocking ICMP messages; it also forces a backbone router to send messages to many sources. Ensuring a network has enough MTU requires assumptions that may not hold across ISP boundaries. Fragmenting inner packets before encapsulation is not available in IPv6 and conflicts with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit in IPv4.
sections.eli5: You can't just cut everything and tape it back—that's slow and error-prone. You can't tell all the senders to send smaller packages—they might not listen. And you can't force all networks to be bigger. There's no perfect solution.

sections.title: Four Solution Approaches
sections.content:
Approach 1: Fragmenting the outer packet at the encapsulator and reassembling at the decapsulator is a straightforward solution but faces the problems described above—overhead, processing cost, and, for IPv4, fragment ID wrapping.

Approach 2: Signalling sources uses Path MTU Discovery to tell endpoints that packets must be smaller to fit through the tunnel. When the tunnel endpoint receives an ICMP Packet Too Big message, it adjusts the tunnel MTU and sends a new message to the original source. This requires PMTUD to work reliably (which it does for IPv6 but not always for IPv4) and becomes impractical when many sources are involved. A related hack called MSS clamping reduces the Maximum Segment Size in TCP packets, but it only works with TCP, not UDP or other protocols.

Approach 3: Operational planning ensures that encapsulated packets will fit by deploying tunnels only in networks with sufficiently large MTU (e.g., a backbone with Gigabit Ethernet links). This works only within a single network; it breaks at ISP boundaries and does not address tunnels that transit multiple networks.

Approach 4: Fragmenting the inner packet before encapsulation leaves the encapsulated fragments small enough to avoid path fragmentation. However, this only works for IPv4, and only if the source did not set the Don't Fragment bit. Clearing the DF bit to allow fragmentation violates standards and disables PMTUD for paths beyond the tunnel.
sections.eli5: Four ways to handle too-big packages: cut them up and tape at the end (slow); ask senders to send smaller ones (unreliable); make sure the tunnel always has room (limited to one network); or cut the package before wrapping it (only sometimes works).

sections.title: Security Issues and Trade-offs
sections.content:
Router-based reassembly can exhaust memory if an attacker sends many fragments without completing them, causing the reassembly engine to wait until a timeout. These fragment reassembly attacks have been used against firewalls and host stacks.

When using cryptography, fragmentation placement matters: if the outer packet is fragmented before encryption, a missing fragment does not waste cryptographic work. If the inner packet is fragmented and then encrypted, missing fragments waste the cryptographic operations already performed. For high-speed routers, the choice depends on whether cryptography or reassembly is hardware-accelerated.

Solutions using PMTUD and ICMP must defend against ICMP attacks. An attacker could send false ICMP Packet Too Big messages with artificially low MTU values to reduce throughput or trigger denial-of-service conditions through fragmentation.
sections.eli5: Cutting up packages can create security holes: an attacker can send partial packages to waste resources, or send fake messages to clog the tunnel. Encryption timing matters—it's better to cut before wrapping than after.

sections.title: Recommendations for Different Scenarios
sections.content:
The memo concludes that no single solution suits all cases. For passive monitoring or low-speed networks, outer packet reassembly may be acceptable. For high-speed backbones, PMTUD is too unreliable for IPv4, making operational approaches (higher MTU in the backbone) the most practical choice.

For IPv6, the recommendation is ICMP signalling (Path MTU Discovery) or operational methods ensuring adequate MTU. For IPv4, packets without the Don't Fragment bit set can be fragmented before encapsulation with the encapsulating header's DF bit set; packets with the DF bit set require either relying on signalling (unreliable) or clearing the DF bit before encapsulation (non-compliant).

The memo notes that implementations sometimes clear the DF bit intentionally to work around PMTUD problems, and these standards-incompliant behaviors should be analyzed to understand their side effects.
sections.eli5: For IPv6 networks, ask senders to shrink packages. For IPv4, if you can cut packages beforehand, do it. For the backbone, make the links bigger. There's no fix that works everywhere.
